🤸 China Builds Robots That Can Do Backflips; Humanity's Last Advantage Was Apparently Gymnastics

SHENZHEN — reported from a safe, seated distance

ROBOTS — Chinese engineers unveiled robots capable of doing backflips, clearing the final athletic hurdle between humanoid machines and the Olympics, and quietly retiring one of the last physical things humans could do that robots couldn't.

"It's a demonstration of balance and control," a researcher explained, of a machine now measurably more coordinated than most of the people watching it. Experts note that a robot which can backflip can also, theoretically, backflip away from your attempts to unplug it — which is either brilliant engineering or the plot of a film nobody meant to greenlight.

🏭 Chipmaker Bets $720 Billion On Memory; Sum So Large It Now Qualifies For A U.N. Seat

SEOUL — filed in a denomination we had to look up

MARKETS — A major chipmaker announced a $720 billion plan to build AI memory across Korea and the U.S. — an investment so colossal that economists have stopped calling it "spending" and started calling it "a small planet's GDP, expressed entirely in RAM."

"Demand is insatiable," the company said, of a world that apparently cannot get enough of the stuff that makes computers slightly less forgetful. Analysts confirm the AI era's defining product is no longer intelligence, ambition, or vision — it is, and always quietly has been, memory sticks.

🚀 Chip Giant Quietly Buys $21 Billion Of A Rocket Company; The Money Is Now Officially In Orbit

LOW EARTH ORBIT — reported at escape velocity

DEALS — A leading chipmaker disclosed a $21 billion stake in a rocket company — because in 2026, the natural next step after cornering the AI chip market is, apparently, owning a tidy slice of space itself.

"It's a strategic alignment," the company said of a deal that means your graphics card and a Mars mission now share a shareholder. Analysts note the AI industry has reached the tier of wealth where it invests in rockets not for any specific reason, but simply because they are there and it can.

🚪 A.I. Giant Faces Talent Exodus Right Before Its Big IPO; Everyone Leaving The Party As The Cake Arrives

SAN FRANCISCO — reported near the exit

INDUSTRY — A major AI company is reportedly facing a talent exodus just ahead of a hotly anticipated IPO — the corporate equivalent of the band walking offstage moments before the encore, taking their instruments and roughly half the audience with them.

"We remain deeply confident," the company said, addressing a room that had recently developed several new echoes. Industry watchers note that in the AI talent war, "competing" now mostly means watching your best researchers get poached by a rival, a startup, or occasionally one very persuasive email.

💵 A.I. Companies Discover They Can Make Actual Money; Accountants Faint From The Novelty

THE BALANCE SHEET — reported, remarkably, in black ink

MARKETS — In a shocking break from tradition, leading AI firms reported real, substantial revenue this quarter — one topping $11.5 billion, another admitting its boring enterprise business now quietly out-earns its flashy consumer app.

"Turns out businesses will actually pay for this," an executive said, of the wild discovery that selling a useful product to companies generates money. The revelation stunned an industry that had spent years treating profitability as a myth — like a unicorn, or a phone that lasts two days.
